rawInput.complaint:
A 66‐year‐old African‐American woman, 4 years after bilateral lung transplantation for end‐stage pulmonary fibrosis, presented with 2 months of progressive dyspnea, wheezing, and 4 weeks of cough productive of scant blood‐tinged sputum. She denied fever or weight loss but reported nightly sweats for 6 months. Her immunosuppression regimen consisted of tacrolimus (goal trough 8–10 ng/mL) and prednisone 5 mg daily; azathioprine had been discontinued years earlier because of pancytopenia. Her medical history included chronic pancytopenia, stage IV chronic kidney disease, diabetes, hypertension, and gastroparesis. 

On examination, she was afebrile, respiratory rate 22/min, oxygen saturation 97% on room air; focal end‐expiratory wheezes were heard over the left lung. Laboratory studies showed pancytopenia (WBC 0.9×10^3/mL, hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, platelets 134×10^3/mL) and elevated creatinine (2.37 mg/dL). CMV and EBV PCR were undetectable. 

Chest CT showed a 2.2×1.1×0.9 cm polypoid soft‐tissue lesion arising from the roof of the left mainstem bronchus at the anastomotic site, with severe luminal narrowing to 3 mm and tree‐in‐bud nodularity in the left lower lobe. 

Rigid bronchoscopy revealed a fibrinous mass protruding into the left mainstem bronchus proximal to the anastomosis. Multiple biopsies were obtained, and a bronchial wash was performed; samples were sent for histopathologic and microbiologic evaluation.

cotDiagnosis.reasoning:
The chief complaint is progressive dyspnea and wheezing over 2 months with 4 weeks of scant hemoptysis in a patient 4 years after bilateral lung transplantation. The patient’s own major concern is worsening airway symptoms, and the imaging localizes this to a focal obstructing lesion in the left mainstem bronchus.

Salient positive findings strongly suggest a focal endobronchial process rather than diffuse parenchymal disease alone. She is chronically immunosuppressed with tacrolimus and prednisone after lung transplant, and also has diabetes and profound chronic pancytopenia with severe leukopenia (WBC 0.9×10^3/mL), all of which increase risk for opportunistic infection and malignancy. Symptoms include progressive dyspnea, focal wheezing over the left lung, scant blood-tinged sputum, and 6 months of nightly sweats. CT shows a 2.2 × 1.1 × 0.9 cm polypoid soft-tissue lesion arising from the roof of the left mainstem bronchus at the anastomotic site, causing severe narrowing to 3 mm, plus tree-in-bud nodularity in the left lower lobe, which can reflect distal endobronchial spread or post-obstructive infectious bronchiolitis. Bronchoscopy directly visualized a fibrinous mass protruding into the left mainstem bronchus proximal to the anastomosis.

Pertinent negatives help refine the differential. She is afebrile, oxygenating well on room air, and denies weight loss. CMV and EBV PCR are undetectable, which makes CMV airway disease and EBV-driven post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder less likely, though not impossible. The lesion is specifically at the bronchial anastomotic site, which is an important clue favoring a transplant-related airway complication or localized infection at a structurally vulnerable site. The focal wheeze and severe unilateral mainstem narrowing argue against simple asthma/COPD-type wheezing. The presence of a discrete endobronchial mass argues against bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome, which causes diffuse small-airway obstruction rather than a visible obstructing bronchial lesion.

The first major differential is post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD). It fits because she is a transplant recipient with night sweats, hemoptysis, and an endobronchial mass. However, PTLD is less favored because the lesion is centered at the anastomotic site and described as fibrinous, there is associated tree-in-bud change suggesting airway-centered infection, and EBV PCR is undetectable. PTLD remains plausible but not the best fit.

The second differential is bronchogenic carcinoma or another endobronchial neoplasm. Hemoptysis, focal wheeze, and a polypoid obstructing lesion are compatible. But the anastomotic location in an immunosuppressed lung transplant recipient, along with the fibrinous appearance and distal tree-in-bud nodularity, makes an infectious pseudotumor-like lesion more likely than primary malignancy.

The third differential is an anastomotic complication such as granulation tissue or bronchial stenosis. The location at the anastomosis and severe luminal narrowing fit well. However, granulation tissue alone would not as readily explain the constitutional symptom of night sweats, hemoptysis, and tree-in-bud nodularity, and the lesion is described as a fibrinous mass rather than simple scar/granulation tissue. In an immunocompromised host, infection superimposed on the anastomosis is more likely.

The fourth and most compelling differential is fungal tracheobronchitis/endobronchial fungal infection, especially Aspergillus involving the bronchial anastomosis. Lung transplant recipients are particularly susceptible to Aspergillus airway infection at bronchial anastomoses because of impaired local vascularity and healing. The case features that support this are: immunosuppression, diabetes, profound leukopenia, a lesion arising at the anastomotic site, bronchoscopic appearance of a fibrinous obstructing mass, hemoptysis, focal wheeze from airway obstruction, and tree-in-bud nodularity distal to the lesion. Aspergillus tracheobronchitis can present as pseudomembranous or obstructing endobronchial masses rather than classic invasive pneumonia, and fever may be absent.

Putting this together, the single most likely diagnosis is obstructing Aspergillus tracheobronchitis at the bronchial anastomosis after lung transplantation. This best explains the focal endobronchial fibrinous mass, severe left mainstem narrowing, distal tree-in-bud changes, and the patient’s immunocompromised post-transplant state.

differentialDiagnoses.condition: Aspergillus tracheobronchitis (endobronchial aspergillosis) at the bronchial anastomosis
differentialDiagnoses.supportingEvidence: Lung transplant recipient on tacrolimus/prednisone with diabetes and severe leukopenia; fibrinous obstructing mass at the left mainstem anastomotic site; hemoptysis, focal wheeze, severe luminal narrowing, and distal tree-in-bud nodularity all support airway-centered fungal infection.

differentialDiagnoses.condition: Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder involving the bronchus
differentialDiagnoses.supportingEvidence: Transplant recipient with night sweats and an endobronchial mass causing obstruction and hemoptysis; however EBV PCR is undetectable and the anastomotic fibrinous appearance with tree-in-bud change favors infection.

Lesion is located at the bronchial anastomosis with severe focal narrowing, which is typical for airway anastomotic complications after lung transplant; less able to explain night sweats and tree-in-bud nodularity without superimposed infection.
Polypoid obstructing lesion with hemoptysis could represent malignancy, but the transplant anastomotic location, fibrinous appearance, and infectious-pattern distal nodularity make this less likely.
